token.def: The unit a language model reads and writes: a whole word, a piece of a word, a punctuation mark or a byte, as its tokenizer splits the text. Cost, speed and context limits are all counted in tokens.

bpe.def: A way to learn a subword vocabulary: start from characters or bytes and repeatedly merge the most frequent adjacent pair into a new token, until the vocabulary reaches its target size.

byte-level-bpe.def: BPE that starts from the 256 byte values instead of characters, so any text, in any script or with emoji, can be encoded without an unknown token.

vocabulary.def: The fixed set of tokens a model knows, each with an id. Modern LLMs use roughly 32,000 to 260,000 tokens.

token-tax.def: The extra tokens a language needs, compared with English, to say the same thing on a given tokenizer. It raises cost and latency and leaves less room in the context window.

attention.def: The operation that lets each token gather information from other tokens: a weighted average of the other tokens' value vectors, weighted by how well the token's query matches each key.

qkv.def: Three vectors computed from each token by learned matrices. The query is what a token looks for, the key is what it offers to be matched on, and the value is what it passes on when matched.

cross-attention.def: Attention in which the queries come from one sequence (the decoder's) and the keys and values from another (the encoder's output).

multi-head-attention.def: Several attentions run in parallel on narrower projections of the same vectors, their outputs concatenated and mixed by one more matrix, so different heads can track different relations.

causal-mask.def: A mask that stops a token attending to later tokens: their scores are set to minus infinity before softmax, so their weights are exactly zero.

positional-encoding.def: Information about each token's position added to a transformer, which would otherwise treat its input as an unordered set.

rope.def: A positional encoding that rotates pairs of query and key dimensions by angles proportional to the position, so the attention score depends only on the distance between two tokens.

residual-stream.def: The vector per token that runs through a transformer. Each sub-layer adds its output to it (a residual connection) instead of replacing it.

rmsnorm.def: Normalisation that divides a vector by its root mean square and multiplies by a learned gain. Pre-norm models apply it before each sub-layer.

ffn.def: The part of a transformer block applied to each position on its own: widen the vector, apply a non-linearity, project back. It holds about two-thirds of a dense model's parameters.

swiglu.def: A feed-forward layer with a gate: one matrix decides how much of a second matrix's output to let through, and a third matrix projects the result back. Used by most current LLMs.

gqa.def: Attention in which groups of query heads share one key head and one value head, which shrinks the KV cache with little loss in quality.

encoder-only.def: A transformer whose tokens all see each other (bidirectional attention), trained to fill in masked tokens. Used for classification, embeddings and rerankers.

decoder-only.def: A transformer with a causal mask, trained to predict the next token. The architecture of GPT-style LLMs.

encoder-decoder.def: A transformer whose bidirectional encoder reads the input and whose causal decoder writes the output, attending to the encoder through cross-attention. Used for translation and speech recognition.

logits.def: The raw, unbounded scores a model outputs, one per vocabulary token, before softmax turns them into probabilities.

softmax.def: The function that turns a vector of scores into probabilities: exponentiate each score and divide by the sum. Adding the same constant to every score changes nothing.

autoregressive.def: Generating one token at a time, each appended to the input before the next is predicted.

prefill-decode.def: The two phases of generation: prefill processes the whole prompt in one parallel pass; decode then produces one token per forward pass.

cross-entropy.def: The training loss of a language model: the average of −log p of the token that actually came next. Lower is better; ln of the vocabulary size is what a uniform guess scores.

kv-cache.def: The keys and values of earlier tokens, kept in memory during generation so each new token only computes its own. It grows linearly with context and is often the memory limit in serving.

temperature.def: A decoding setting that divides logits before softmax: below 1 sharpens the distribution, above 1 flattens it, and towards 0 it approaches greedy decoding.

greedy-decoding.def: Always choosing the most probable next token.

top-k.def: Sampling only from the k most probable tokens, after renormalising their probabilities.

top-p.def: Sampling only from the smallest set of tokens whose probabilities add up to at least p, after renormalising.

moe.def: A model in which each feed-forward layer is replaced by many expert networks and a router that sends each token to a few of them, so most parameters are stored but not used for any one token.

router.def: The small learned layer in a mixture-of-experts model that scores the experts for each token and picks the top few.

active-parameters.def: The parameters a model actually uses for one token. In a dense model it is all of them; in an MoE model it is the shared layers plus the chosen experts.

context-window.def: The maximum number of tokens, prompt and output together, a model can attend to in one request.

artificial-intelligence.def: Any technique that makes a computer do a task we would call intelligent if a person did it, such as planning, recognising or deciding. Hand-written rules count.

machine-learning.def: AI whose behaviour is learned from examples instead of written by hand.

deep-learning.def: Machine learning with neural networks of many layers, which learn their own intermediate features from data.

generative-ai.def: Models that create new content, such as text, images, audio or code, by learning what their training data looks like and producing new examples of it.

foundation-model.def: One large model pretrained on broad data and then adapted to many tasks, instead of one model trained per task.

agent.def: An LLM that works in a loop: it chooses a tool, looks at the result and decides the next step, until the task is done or a limit is reached.

language-model.def: A model that gives a probability to every possible next token, given the text so far. Generating text means picking a token, adding it and repeating.

llm.def: A transformer language model with billions of parameters, pretrained on a very large and broad text collection.

parameter.def: One learned number inside a model, also called a weight. An 8B model has about 8 billion of them.

embedding.def: A list of numbers (a vector) that stands for a token or a piece of text, so that similar meanings get similar numbers.

tokenizer.def: The part that splits text into tokens and turns them into id numbers. Each model family has its own, so the same text is a different number of tokens on different models.

training-inference.def: Training changes a model's parameters so its predictions improve; it is expensive and rare. Inference uses fixed parameters to answer; it is cheap per call and happens constantly.

hallucination.def: Fluent, confident output that is false, such as an invented citation, flag or policy clause.

training-cutoff.def: The date the training data ends. A model knows nothing after it unless the facts are put into its input.

grounding.def: Giving the model the source facts in its input and asking it to answer from them, with citations, so the answer can be checked.

vector.def: An ordered list of numbers, such as [0.2, -1.3, 0.7]. It can be pictured as an arrow; an embedding is a vector with hundreds or thousands of numbers.

cosine-similarity.def: How closely two vectors point the same way, from 1 (same direction) through 0 (unrelated) to -1 (opposite). It ignores their lengths, so it compares meaning rather than size.

base-rate.def: How common something is before any test, such as the share of transactions that are fraud. When it is low, most alarms from even a good detector are false.

confidence-interval.def: A range around a measured number that shows how far it could be off because only a sample was tested. More test cases make it narrower.

gradient.def: For each parameter, which way and how steeply the loss changes when that parameter grows a little.

gradient-descent.def: Training by many small steps: move every parameter a little in the direction that lowers the loss, then repeat.

learning-rate.def: How big each gradient-descent step is. Too small and training crawls; too big and it overshoots and can blow up.

loss-function.def: One number that says how wrong a model is on some examples. Training tries to make it smaller.

entropy.def: How unpredictable outcomes are, on average, measured in bits. A fair coin is 1 bit; a coin that always lands heads is 0.

kl-divergence.def: The extra surprise you pay for using a wrong guess of the probabilities instead of the true ones. Zero only when the guess is exactly right.

perplexity.def: A language model's loss turned into 'how many equally likely tokens it is choosing between'. Lower is better.

vectorisation.def: Writing a calculation as one operation on a whole array instead of a Python loop, so fast compiled code does the work.

reproducibility.def: Getting the same result again from the same inputs, which needs fixed seeds and recorded versions of code, data, models and prompts.

tensor.def: An array with any number of dimensions: a number, a vector, a matrix, or more, such as batch × tokens × features.

memory-bandwidth.def: How many bytes per second can be read from memory. Generating a token reads every weight once, so it often limits LLM speed more than raw compute does.

bf16.def: A 2-byte number format with the same range as 4-byte float32 but fewer digits of precision. The usual format for training and serving LLMs.

supervised-learning.def: Learning from examples that come with the right answer (a label), such as emails marked spam or not spam.

unsupervised-learning.def: Finding structure, such as groups or unusual items, in data that has no labels.

self-supervised-learning.def: Making labels from the data itself, such as hiding the next word and predicting it. It is how LLMs learn from trillions of tokens without human labelling.

reinforcement-learning.def: Learning by trying actions and getting rewards, so that actions that earned more reward become more likely.

baseline.def: The simplest sensible way to do a task, such as always giving the most common answer. A model is only worth what it adds over its baseline.

gradient-boosting.def: An ensemble that adds small decision trees one at a time, each fixing the errors of the ones before. Usually the strongest choice for tables of data.

k-means.def: A clustering method that repeats two steps: put each point with its nearest centre, then move each centre to the middle of its points.

class-imbalance.def: When one outcome is much rarer than the others, so a model can ignore it and still score high accuracy.

feature-engineering.def: Turning raw data into useful model inputs, such as a date into 'day of the week' or transactions into 'count in the last 24 hours'.

inter-annotator-agreement.def: How often two people labelling the same items agree, beyond what chance would give. Low agreement means the task itself is unclear.

overfitting.def: Learning the training examples so closely, noise included, that the model does worse on new data.

regularisation.def: Anything that stops a model fitting too closely, such as a penalty on large weights, limiting tree depth, dropout or stopping early.

data-leakage.def: Information in training data that would not be available when the model is really used, which makes test scores look better than real use will be.

train-validation-test.def: Three separate parts of the data: one to learn from, one to choose settings with, and one kept back to estimate real performance once.

precision-recall.def: Precision: of everything flagged, the share that was right. Recall: of everything that should have been flagged, the share that was caught.

f1.def: One number that combines precision and recall; it is high only when both are high.

calibration.def: Whether a model's scores mean what they say: of the cases scored 0.8, about 80% should really be positive.

error-analysis.def: Reading a sample of a model's mistakes, tagging each with a cause and counting the causes, so you fix the biggest one first.

hyperparameter.def: A setting chosen before training rather than learned, such as the learning rate or tree depth.

distribution-shift.def: When the data a model sees in use differs from the data it was trained on, such as new customers, new products or new kinds of fraud.

neuron.def: The basic unit of a neural network: multiply each input by a weight, add them up with a bias, and pass the result through an activation function.

activation-function.def: The bend applied after a neuron's weighted sum, such as ReLU or GELU. Without it, any number of layers acts like a single straight-line layer.

backpropagation.def: Working out every weight's gradient by applying the chain rule backwards from the loss through the layers, reusing the values saved on the way forward.

epoch.def: A batch is the group of examples used for one update, a step is one update, and an epoch is one full pass over the training data.

adamw.def: The default optimiser for transformers: it keeps a running average of each parameter's gradient and of its square, and gives every parameter its own step size. AdamW handles weight decay separately.

lr-schedule.def: Changing the learning rate during training; for LLMs, usually a short warm-up from near zero followed by a slow cosine decay.

gradient-accumulation.def: Adding up gradients over several small batches before one update, to act like a bigger batch than fits in memory.

vanishing-gradients.def: Gradients that shrink towards zero or grow without limit as they pass back through many layers, so early layers stop learning or training blows up.

normalisation.def: A layer that rescales activations to a steady size: BatchNorm across a batch, LayerNorm and RMSNorm within one example.

dropout.def: Switching off a random share of activations at each training step so the network cannot rely on any single path. It is turned off when the model is used.

gradient-clipping.def: Scaling the gradient down when its size passes a limit, often 1.0, to stop one bad batch causing a huge update.

representation-learning.def: A network learning useful internal vectors for its inputs as a side effect of its training task.

contrastive-learning.def: Training an encoder by pulling matching pairs (a question and its answer) together and pushing non-matching pairs apart. How text embedding models are trained.

cnn.def: A network that slides small learned filters across an image or sequence, finding the same local pattern wherever it appears.

rnn.def: A network that reads a sequence one step at a time and carries a hidden state forward. LSTMs and GRUs add gates so the state fades less.

autograd.def: A framework feature that records the operations you run and works out all the gradients for you when you call backward().

checkpoint.def: A saved copy of a model's weights, optimiser state and step number, so training can resume or the best version can be kept.

pretraining.def: The first and by far the most expensive training stage: next-token prediction on trillions of tokens of general text. It produces a base model.

base-model.def: A model straight out of pretraining. It continues text well but does not reliably follow instructions.

sft.def: Training a model on example conversations (instruction and good answer) so it learns to behave as an assistant or follow a format.

continued-pretraining.def: More next-token training on domain text, such as law, code or a new language, to shift what a model knows.

deduplication.def: Removing exact and near-duplicate documents from training data, usually with hashes and MinHash, so the model does not waste compute or memorise repeats.

contamination.def: Test or benchmark questions appearing in the training data, which makes scores on them meaningless.

data-mixture.def: The share of each source in training data, such as web, code, books and maths. It shapes what the model is good at.

scaling-laws.def: Measured rules for how loss falls as parameters, training tokens and compute grow; they let teams predict a big run from small ones.

mfu.def: The share of a GPU's peak arithmetic speed a training run really uses; 35–50% is typical for large runs.

chat-template.def: The exact text format, with special role tokens, that turns a list of chat messages into the token sequence a model was trained on.

loss-masking.def: Computing the training loss only on the tokens the model should learn to write, usually the assistant's replies, and ignoring the rest.

reward-model.def: A model trained on preference comparisons to give an answer a score for how good it is.

rlhf.def: Reinforcement learning from human feedback: generate answers, score them with a reward model and update the LLM to score higher, while a penalty keeps it close to the original.

dpo.def: Direct preference optimisation: training straight on pairs of preferred and rejected answers, with no separate reward model or RL loop.

rlvr.def: Reinforcement learning where the reward is checked automatically, such as unit tests passing or a maths answer matching. GRPO is a common algorithm for it.

reward-hacking.def: A model learning to score well on the reward without doing the task better, such as padding answers if longer ones score higher.

data-parallelism.def: Training with a full copy of the model on every GPU, each on different batches, averaging the gradients after every step.

zero-fsdp.def: Data parallelism that splits the optimiser state, gradients and even the weights across GPUs instead of copying them, so much bigger models fit.

tensor-parallelism.def: Splitting each big weight matrix across several GPUs so they share every layer's work. It needs very fast links between the GPUs.

pipeline-parallelism.def: Putting different layers on different GPUs and passing micro-batches through them like an assembly line; some GPUs wait at the start and end.

open-weights.def: A model whose trained weights you can download and run on your own hardware, as opposed to one you can only call through a provider's API.

few-shot.def: Putting a handful of worked input-and-output examples in the prompt so the model copies the format and decisions.

system-prompt.def: The developer's standing instructions sent with every request, separate from the user's message.

prompt-versioning.def: Storing prompts with an id and version, reviewing and testing every change, and logging the version with every request.

context-engineering.def: Deciding, for every model call, exactly what goes into the context window and in what order, within a token budget.

structured-output.def: Asking the model to answer as data in a declared format, usually JSON matching a schema, so code can read it.

constrained-decoding.def: Blocking any token that would break a schema or grammar while the model generates, so the output always has the right shape. It does not make the content true.

tool-calling.def: The model answering with a request to run a named function with arguments; your code checks it, runs it and sends back the result.

streaming.def: Sending the answer token by token as it is generated, so users see the first words sooner.

stateless-api.def: An API that remembers nothing between calls, so the application must send the whole conversation it wants the model to know every time.

compaction.def: Shrinking a long conversation's history by summarising old turns and extracting key facts, so it keeps fitting the context window.

exponential-backoff.def: Waiting longer after each failed attempt (1, 2, 4, 8 seconds), with a random part, so many clients do not retry at the same moment.

token-bucket.def: A rate limiter that refills a fixed number of allowances per second up to a maximum; requests wait until enough are available.

fallback.def: What happens when the main model keeps failing: a second model or provider, a cached answer or a polite message. It needs evaluating too.

deterministic-boundary.def: The line between what a model suggests and what code decides: the model interprets and proposes, rules in code check, decide and act.
